items.t: Caterpillar stock faces capacity test after record Q3 sales
sum: Caterpillar's record third quarter shifted the investor focus from demand to execution. The company reported the results on October 29, while Utility Dive described the capacity response to data-center demand in a report published November 3.

According to Caterpillar's earnings release, third-quarter sales and revenues rose 17 percent year over year to 20.7 billion US dollars. Profit per share was 7.13 US dollars, while adjusted profit per share reached 7.20 US dollars after excluding restructuring costs.

Operating profit margin improved to 20.4 percent from 17.3 percent a year earlier. Caterpillar also deployed 2.0 billion US dollars for share repurchases and dividends during the quarter, including 1.2 billion US dollars of buybacks and 0.7 billion US dollars of dividends.

Utility Dive reported that Caterpillar's backlog reached 78 billion US dollars, nearly double the year-earlier level. The publication said the company is expanding production of large reciprocating engines and turbines to serve data-center customers.

Power and Energy sales rose 18 percent to 8.8 billion US dollars in the third quarter, with power-generation sales up 30 percent year over year. The division's growth highlights the opportunity, but capacity expansion, delivery timing and manufacturing costs remain important execution issues for investors.

Caterpillar expects moderate sales growth in the fourth quarter and higher operating profit margins. For the full year, management maintained a mid-to-high-teens sales-growth outlook and estimated tariff costs of about 2.2 billion US dollars, excluding refunds.

Caterpillar posted record revenue and backlog but its stock still fell
sum: Caterpillar beat Wall Street on every major number Wednesday. Investors sold the stock anyway. The company that makes bulldozers is now, by its own numbers, running on diesel generators and turbines for AI data centers as much as on construction equipment.

Caterpillar reported third-quarter revenue of $20.68 billion on October 29, up 17% from a year earlier. Good numbers. Adjusted earnings came in at $7.20 a share against a Wall Street estimate of roughly $7.03 to $7.06, according to figures reported by Alphastreet and Investing.com. The backlog, the pile of orders not yet shipped, hit a record $72 billion, up $9 billion from the prior quarter. CEO Joe Creed called it a result of "strong order rates and a record backlog." None of it stopped the stock from falling. Shares dropped as much as 12% in the session, according to tikr.com, after sliding roughly 7.6% in premarket trading.

Caterpillar's Energy & Transportation segment, the unit that builds engines, turbines and standby generators, posted sales of $8.78 billion, up 18% year over year. Within that, Power Generation sales climbed 33% to 44% depending on how the comparison is drawn, driven almost entirely by reciprocating engines and turbines sold to data center operators. Hyperscale customers, the Amazons and Microsofts of the world building out their own server farms, now account for roughly 35% of Energy & Transportation orders, up from 22% a year ago.

That's the part of this earnings report that actually matters for anyone trying to understand where AI money is flowing. Nvidia and the chipmakers get the headlines, but somebody has to keep the lights on and the servers cool. Increasingly that somebody is Caterpillar. A hyperscale data center doesn't just need GPUs. It needs megawatts, often more than the local grid can promise on a reasonable timeline, which is why operators are turning to on-site generation. Caterpillar's reciprocating engines and turbines fill that gap. The company says 59% of its record backlog is scheduled to ship within 12 months: this isn't a speculative pipeline, it's revenue already booked.
Tariffs, mostly. Caterpillar has told investors to expect $2.2 billion to $2.4 billion in tariff costs for 2026.

items.t: Is Caterpillar Stock’s Winning Streak Skill Or Luck?
sum: For questions about this article or underlying research, email help@trefis.com.

Caterpillar Inc. (CAT), the maker of construction machines, engines and turbines, has beaten the S&P 500 in each of the last five years. A record like that looks like the mark of an exceptional company. Of about 480 large U.S. stocks, how many do you think managed the same streak?
Caterpillar shares beat the index in every one of the five twelve-month periods since October 2021, including the first, when both fell.
Price changes over periods of 252 trading sessions each, dividends excluded.

Only 8 of the 485 current S&P 500 members with five years of prices have a streak that long. That is rarer than it sounds, because a single stock usually loses to the index. In the latest year, only 42.3% of them beat it. Beating the index once is already the less common outcome, and doing it five years running is rare.

When dealing with this many stocks, a few will put together long streaks even if no company is any better than another. About four in ten of these stocks beat the index in a typical year. Suppose it were pure luck which ones did. That would mean putting all 485 names in a hat each year and drawing a little over four in ten of them as that year’s winners.
Do that five years in a row, and about six names come out every single time. Those six companies would have a five-year winning streak with no skill involved at all.

sum: Industrial-equipment maker Caterpillar CAT faces a test of its AI power-demand story when earnings arrive before Thursday's opening bell. Shares stood at $693.395 Monday, approximately 0.93% higher, at 11:15 a.m. ET. Kiplinger puts Wall Street's expectations at $7.03 per share on $20.7 billion in revenue. Investors need evidence that demand for data-center power equipment can sustain fresh orders.

The backlog offers visibility, but its timing deserves scrutiny. Bernstein analyst Chad Dillard, cited in Kiplinger's preview, says orders scheduled beyond 12 months now account for nearly 40% of backlog, versus roughly 20% historically. He also says construction of data centers using behind-the-meter power has remained around 15 gigawatts since May, raising questions about future bookings. That distinction matters: existing orders can support near-term sales even as new demand slows.

The valuation leaves a demanding hurdle: the $693.395 share price sits 48.08% above the $468.25 GF Value estimate. That premium does not establish where shares should trade next, but it increases the importance of execution. Thursday's report needs to show how quickly backlog converts into revenue, whether margins hold and whether incoming orders replenish completed work. An earnings beat would carry more weight if fresh bookings support the next stretch of growth.

sum: Caterpillar heads into its third-quarter report with an unusual disconnect. Three months ago the company posted its first quarter above $20 billion in sales, raised its full-year revenue outlook for the third straight time and pointed to a record $72 billion backlog. Since then the stock has fallen about 21%, trailing the S&P 500 by more than 22 percentage points. Either the market is looking past the good news toward a peak, or it has punished a company whose fundamentals are still moving in the right direction. The October 29 report, due before the open, should help settle which view is closer to the truth.

The Street expects earnings of $7.12 a share on revenue of about $20.17 billion. That would be roughly 44% EPS growth and 14% sales growth from a year ago, which is strong by any industrial standard. On a sequential basis, though, both figures sit below the second quarter's $8.17 and $20.54 billion. That dip is easy to explain. The prior quarter benefited from $392 million in IEPA tariff recoveries that management does not expect to repeat in the second half. Without that boost, margins were tracking only near the bottom of the company's target range, weighed down by depreciation from new capacity, freight costs and heavier spending on SG&A and R&D. The whisper number of $7.24 sits a bit above consensus. That suggests some expectation of an upside surprise, but not a dramatically higher bar.

The most important evidence will come from the backlog and the guidance. Order books have climbed every quarter, from $39.8 billion a year ago to $72 billion, and last quarter all three segments contributed rather than Power & Energy alone. Another increase, or even holding near that level as shipments accelerate, would support management's view that data center customers are ordering out to 2030 with no signs of slowing. A noticeable decline would feed the doubts analysts raised last quarter about how long AI-driven demand can last. The same logic applies to the sales outlook. Management lifted it from roughly the top of a 5% to 7% growth range, to low double digits, to mid-to-high teens. After three raises, simply reaffirming may read as a pause. A fourth increase would argue that momentum is still building.

Caterpillar (CAT) and Deere (DE) Slide as Treasury Yields Surge. Why Valuations Matter
sum: On October 7, Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT) slid as much as 7% to around $807-$813, with Deere & Company (NYSE:DE) down 4% to roughly $658 as the 30-year Treasury yield climbed to 5.7%, its highest level in over two decades. Industrial stocks were among the hardest-hit sectors, while the S&P 500 finished down approximately 0.2%, reflecting broader pressure from rising Treasury yields alongside concerns about a federal inquiry into competition in the agricultural equipment industry.

Caterpillar was the single most significant drag on the Dow, which fell 341 points, or 0.7%, to 51,180. With Caterpillar and Deere facing valuation pressure, investors may want to look beyond heavy machinery. See which 8 industrial stocks offer opportunities for investors in 2026

The mechanism is simple: heavy equipment is typically purchased on credit, whether by construction firms financing a fleet of excavators or farmers financing a combine, so when long-term borrowing costs rise, the effective price of that equipment rises alongside them, regardless of how strong current order books appear. That's why industrials as a whole fell more than three times compared to the broader market, and Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT), the largest and most valuable name in the sector, took the worst hit.

The most important aspect, however, is that both stocks were already trading at high multiples before the October 7 selloff, which alters how this selloff should be read. Caterpillar traded at approximately 37.1 times trailing earnings on October 6, before the selloff, above even the standards of an industrial sector trading well above its historical norms, with a forward multiple in the mid-20s. Deere's multiples were also similarly inflated, despite Deere's agricultural end-markets currently experiencing a cyclical slump rather than a demand boom. The valuation concerns aren't new: at the end of June, Michael Burry announced a short position in Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE:CAT) at $1,060.98, claiming that the stock's AI-driven surge had inflated its valuation beyond what its underlying earnings could support.
However, the two stocks don't have equal exposure to the same story.

🚩 Caterpillar shares extend decline, down 30% from record high
sum: Caterpillar (CAT.US) shares are down around 5.5%, making the stock the weakest performer in the Dow Jones Industrial Average. The immediate catalyst for the sell-off was a price-target cut by Truist Securities from $1,225 to $1,100, although analysts maintained a Buy rating. The bank pointed to concerns over the durability of spending tied to power generation, data centers and artificial intelligence, as well as the negative impact of high interest rates and rising diesel prices.

Today’s decline, however, follows a very strong rally. Caterpillar shares are still up more than 50% year to date, outperforming the Nasdaq 100 and S&P 500 by nearly three times, which makes the stock more vulnerable to profit-taking and valuation concerns. Investors will now focus mainly on the company’s Q3 earnings, which are expected at the end of October.

Investors increasingly view Caterpillar as one of the major beneficiaries of AI-related capital spending, with meaningful exposure to data-center construction. The shares have fallen by around 30% from their local peak and are now trading close to the 200-day exponential moving average, EMA200 (red line). Caterpillar is scheduled to report earnings on October 29 after the US market close. The market is no longer valuing the company like a typical cyclical industrial manufacturer, but rather as a business expected to deliver sustained growth from power generation, infrastructure and data-center investment.

From a valuation perspective, Caterpillar is a classic example of a company whose strong share-price performance appears to have moved ahead of the pace of fundamental improvement. The stock has gained around 42% year to date and nearly 65% over the past 12 months, while average growth over the last eight quarters stands at roughly 3.5% for revenue, 4.5% for EBIT and just 1.1% for EPS. With a trailing P/E of 37 and a forward P/E of around 32, the market is paying a substantial premium for further earnings improvement and the continuation of a strong investment cycle. On the other hand, the company continues to show strong operating quality, with an EBIT margin of around 20.9% and ROE of 75.5%, pointing to very high profitability on equity.

sum: While the market was focused on its slowing construction business, one of Caterpillar’s divisions was quietly building a record-breaking order book that hinted at the rally to come.

It’s easy to look at a stock chart after a 132% run and feel like you missed the party. Caterpillar (CAT)’s surge over the past year was the kind of move that turns heads and mints money. But looking back, was the invitation simply lost in the mail, or was it written in a language most investors weren’t reading?

If you were just scanning the headlines before the run, you’d be forgiven for shrugging. As of its fiscal Q1 2025 report, Caterpillar’s overall revenue was actually down 5.6% over the prior year, a continued deceleration from its recent trend. On the surface, this looked more like a company gearing down than one about to take off. The real story, however, was buried a level deeper.

The tell was hiding in the company’s Energy & Transportation segment. For quarters, management had been dropping hints. As early as the second quarter of 2024, they noted that this specific division was the primary driver of an increase in the company’s total order backlog. By the third quarter of 2024, they were being more explicit, stating that the strength was being “driven by data center growth related to cloud computing and generative AI.” While the iconic yellow bulldozers were in a soft patch, the engines powering the new tech economy were in high demand. For more on the forces behind the company’s performance, it’s worth exploring what engine was truly driving Caterpillar’s run.

The slow build culminated in a notable disclosure in the company’s fiscal Q1 2025 earnings call, the last one before the stock began its ascent. Management reported a $5 billion jump in the backlog in a single quarter, calling it an “all-time record for organic backlog growth.” The driver was, once again, Energy & Transportation. In that same quarter, sales to users for power generation equipment grew by 58%, which the company linked directly to “demand for reciprocating engines for data center applications.” The signal was as clear as a neon sign.
Almost nothing. In the weeks leading up to the surge, options traders were pricing in low levels of calm.

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a version of the Zacks Consensus whose definition is related to change. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

sum: Shares of Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE: CAT) have climbed 175% over the past 12 months and are up 84% year-to-date, trading near $1,069 — a stunning run that has pushed the 100-year-old heavy equipment maker’s market capitalization to approximately $459 billion and earned it a spot in the newly rebalanced Russell Top 50 Index.

The rally reflects a powerful convergence of secular tailwinds. Chief among them is surging demand for Caterpillar’s natural gas turbines and industrial engines to power AI data centers. The company is a key supplier in high-profile projects, including a Chevron-Microsoft initiative to build dedicated power infrastructure for large-scale AI compute facilities. Analysts note that data center developers, unable to wait years for utility grid upgrades, are turning to Caterpillar’s on-site power solutions to bridge a widening electricity gap.

That demand is visible in the numbers. Caterpillar reported a record $63 billion order backlog in Q1 2026, and management raised its full-year 2026 revenue growth outlook to low double digits. Quarterly revenue grew 22% year-over-year, while earnings surged 30%, pushing trailing EPS to $20.05 — with Wall Street forecasting $24.60 for full-year 2026 and $30.11 in 2027.

Beyond AI infrastructure, Caterpillar is benefiting from robust U.S. government infrastructure spending, a mining equipment replacement cycle tied to the global energy transition, and a recovering manufacturing sector that has now posted six consecutive months of expansion.

Shareholders are also being rewarded directly: the company recently raised its quarterly dividend by 8% to $1.63 per share, targeting $30 billion in services revenue by 2030. A Supreme Court ruling that struck down broad U.S. tariffs has further brightened the outlook, with Caterpillar among companies expected to receive meaningful import-duty refunds.

With a forward P/E of 41x and EV/Sales exceeding 6x — well above the company’s historical range of 2–4x — some value-oriented investors have flagged valuation risk. But for now, Wall Street’s bull case, powered by AI, infrastructure and energy, shows little sign of slowing down.
